bio: Babur Ayub is a seasoned professional who has led major brands in Pakistan and now works as a business consultant, corporate trainer, lecturer, and actor. Born and raised in Lahore, he studied at FC College and did his MBA in Lahore, started his career as Operations Head Pakistan at ChenOne, and went on to serve as GM and chief operating officer at various brands.

In this episode he traces Pakistan's downfall to moral decline and a lack of professionalism, talks about traffic and LDA failure, mental tension in daily life, his journey as an actor, the Lazawal Ishq serial, the discussion around Article 295-C, and how the nation can rise from here.

summary: In Episode 6 of Muffled Minds, host Khawar Shahzad sits down with Babur Ayub, a seasoned professional who has led major brands in Pakistan and now works as a business consultant, corporate trainer, lecturer, and actor. Born and raised in Lahore, Babur started his career as Operations Head Pakistan at ChenOne and went on to serve as GM and chief operating officer at various brands, before adding acting to a career built on business development, advising, and corporate training.

The conversation opens with the reasons behind Pakistan's downfall: moral deterioration, a social fiber whose foundationing went wrong, and a mindset that does not accept growth. Babur talks about dua and treatment, the fabricated stories children are raised on, the Gallup survey that found 90 percent of boys dream of a good marriage, and the absence of professionalism, from the Usain Bolt example to the WAPDA front desk. Then comes the daily cost of it all: mental tension, traffic as a trigger of anxiety and depression, and institutions like LDA failing to deliver while Lahore floods.

Part two turns to Babur's journey as an actor, the dark side of the entertainment industry, and the Lazawal Ishq serial, before a long discussion around Article 295-C: what the law was made for, how it is misused for grudges, income, and virality, and why respect between human beings matters as much as the law itself. He closes with how the nation can rise: accept the truth, value time, and take ownership, ending with the fish-jar question about what he is struggling with in his day-to-day life.

takeaways: Mentally we do not accept growth: the downfall starts in the mindset, not in the system.
Dua is a concentration exercise, not a substitute for treatment: dua ke saath dawa ki bhi zaroorat hoti hai.
Bad experiences and fabricated stories shape you; question what you were raised on.
Professionalism is ethics and etiquette in daily life, from the front desk to the boardroom.
Traffic and broken institutions are not just inconvenience: they are silent triggers of anxiety and depression.
A law made to protect respect can be misused for grudges, income, and virality; verify before you accuse.
Respect between human beings matters as much as any law; prophets are not disgraced by small talk.
Rise by accepting the truth, valuing your time, and taking ownership of the work that is overdue.
